Good morning. Look at these students. Every one of them walked into a campus like yours this morning, carrying a family's hopes and a bag full of questions. Across the JNTU family, JNTU Anantapur, JNTU Kakinada, JNTU Hyderabad, JNTU-GV Vizianagaram and JNAFAU, there are about 586 affiliated colleges that we are bringing together. Different buildings, different principals, different traditions. Today I want to give all of us one direction. Not a scheme. Not a circular. A direction: where our students go, what they can do when they get there, and how fast. Give me twenty minutes and I will show you exactly what that looks like.

The gap. Measured in years.
20062026 Where we are Where they are
Let me start with an uncomfortable truth. On the left is an engineering college classroom in India, one many of us know well. On the right is Tokyo. In technology and research, countries like Japan and the UK are roughly twenty years ahead of us. That is not a judgement on our teachers or our students. Our students are as sharp as anyone on earth. The gap is in tools, exposure and systems. And a gap measured in years can be closed in years. That is the work. We intend to close a large part of those twenty years in this decade, starting with the 586 campuses represented in this room.
Our problems. Researched elsewhere.
20 years ahead · one record per sector
Education · USAMIT: world's No. 1 university, 14 years running
Healthcare · UK500,000 whole genomes sequenced for research
Transport · JapanBullet trains since 1964. No passenger deaths.
Green energy · Germany56% of public power from renewables
Innovation · SwitzerlandNo. 1 on innovation, 15 years. India: 38th.
R&D, % of GDP · USA 3.5 · Japan 3.4 · Germany 3.1 · India 0.65
Sources: QS via MIT News 2026 · UK Biobank 2023 · JR Central · Fraunhofer ISE 2025
WIPO Global Innovation Index 2025 · US NCSES / national R&D statistics
Here is what stings. Some of the most important research about India, about our farms, our health and our cities, is being written in the USA, the UK, Germany, Switzerland and Japan. They study our problems because they have the labs, the data and the habit of research. Look at what twenty years of that habit has built, sector by sector. In education, MIT has been ranked the number one university in the world for fourteen years in a row. In healthcare, the UK has sequenced the complete genomes of half a million volunteers for researchers to use. In transport, Japan's bullet trains have run since 1964 without a single passenger killed on board in an accident. In green energy, more than half of Germany's public electricity now comes from renewables. And Switzerland has topped the Global Innovation Index for fifteen straight years, while India stands at thirty-eighth. They spend three to three and a half percent of GDP on research; we spend about 0.65 percent. We will bring the research papers from these countries to our students, and build the habit here. Imagine a final-year student in Anantapur or Kakinada writing the paper that solves a problem in her own district. Our problems, researched here, by our own students.

Why Microsoft? Because that is where the world works. More than 450 million people pay for Microsoft 365 at work. Teams alone has more than 320 million monthly users. More than 90 percent of the Fortune 500 now use Microsoft 365 Copilot, and over 30 million Copilot seats are already paid for. Every lit window in this building is a Fortune 500 company on Microsoft; only one floor in ten is dark. Walk into any large company, in Hyderabad, Bengaluru or Boston, and you will find Teams, Excel, Outlook and Azure. The rest of the world has standardised on these tools. Most of our campuses have not, and that is part of the twenty-year gap. When our students learn on what industry runs on, they do not need six months of training after they are hired. They are productive on day one.

Microsoft 365 is not just a workplace suite. It is built for campuses, in three layers. For students: Learning Accelerators like Reading and Math Progress, study agents, and Copilot Chat with guardrails that push students to think rather than copy. For faculty: help with course planning, grading and drafting assessments. For campus IT: Intune for Education, Entra ID and Purview, which secure every device and every identity from one console. The numbers back it up. Forrester, in a study commissioned by Microsoft, found a 161 percent return on investment for higher-education institutions on Microsoft 365 A5. Microsoft's 2025 AI in Education report found that 93 percent of students and 87 percent of educators have already used AI for school. In one Copilot pilot in Brisbane, educators saved over nine hours a week. Now look at the right. These are the skills employers expect on day one: data literacy, security and compliance, and workflow automation. The world's workplaces already run on these tools. Most of our campuses don't, so our graduates spend their first months catching up. We intend to end that.

This is what it looks like on a student's laptop. Excel for their lab data. Word for their project reports. Teams for classes, reviews, client calls and interviews. The same tools, the same shortcuts and the same habits they will use at work. A student who has spent four years collaborating on Teams and building models in Excel walks into an interview already speaking the language of the workplace. And for the engineers, JetBrains: IntelliJ IDEA, PyCharm and the rest of the professional IDEs the world's top companies build with. 88 of the Fortune Global 100 use JetBrains, so it is the everyday IDE across the Fortune 500. Our students will build real projects in real codebases with the same IDE, the same debugger and the same tests a big company uses, so the first project at work is not the first project they have ever shipped. Hands-on experience, from the first semester. Trained on day-one tools.
We'll know what's used. And what isn't.
One Microsoft cloud · lit by use
Giving licences is easy. Making sure they are used is the real job. And Microsoft is not three apps; it is a whole cloud. In the first circle is Microsoft 365: Teams, Word, Excel, PowerPoint, Outlook, OneDrive and SharePoint. In the second is Dynamics 365, the business applications companies run on: sales, customer service, finance and supply chain. In the third is Azure and Entra: identity, device management, security and Azure AI. Where Microsoft 365 meets Dynamics sits the Power Platform, Power BI, Power Apps and Power Automate. And at the centre, touching all three, are Copilot and the AI agents built on top of it. We will analyse usage across every institution and every circle. The brighter an app, the more it is used. This is sample data, but a pattern like this tells us where to run training, which tools to push and where to spend money. No guesswork. We will know what is used and what is not, and we will act on it.

Let me put it plainly: what problems are we actually solving? First, tools. Our graduates learn the tools industry uses only after they get hired. We put Microsoft 365 and JetBrains in their hands from day one. Second, usage. Too often licences are bought and then nobody uses them. We measure usage across the whole Microsoft cloud and act on it. Third, support. When IT breaks the night before an exam, help should not wait until Monday, so we support every institution twenty-four by seven. Fourth, jobs. Most campuses see few real projects and few real jobs. We have a thousand roles reserved for JNTU students. Fifth, exposure. The best professors and labs are far away, so we bring them to all 586 campuses through live seminars, and take students abroad. Sixth, ideas. Good student ideas die without money or mentors. Hackathons, mentors and a startup fund change that. And finally, cost. World-class tools are expensive, so Lokha carries seventy to seventy-five percent of it. What’s broken, and how we fix it.
Problems in. Solutions out. On loop.
Agents in the loop
Microsoft Copilot ChatGPT Gemini Claude
We are also using AI the way it should be used: to solve real problems. We find a problem, at a client, at an institution or in a process. We build a solution. We automate it so it runs on its own. Then we feed what we learned back in and find the next problem. Problems go in, solutions come out, and the loop keeps running. Inside the loop we use the leading AI models, Microsoft Copilot, ChatGPT, Gemini and Claude, but a general chatbot does not know a client's data, rules or customers. So for every client we plan and build a custom agent around their problem, using whichever model fits it best. Our students learn by working inside these loops, on real client work.

And the work is real. We have around a thousand job opportunities on our own projects, ready to deploy, and they are reserved for JNTU students. Every dot here is a role filled by one of your students. The ones who work hardest, who show up, finish what they start and ask the next question, move onto the intern track and grow with us. The path from your classroom to a real job runs through our projects. One thousand jobs, ready to deploy, only for JNTU students.

Here is one example of what that network makes possible. When a top professor from abroad gives a seminar, a guest lecture or a workshop, we stream it live to every engineering college in the network, and students anywhere in the world can join in. A student in Anantapur sits in the same session as a student in Kakinada, Hyderabad, or London, in real time, with the professor explaining every step and taking their questions. The same channel carries international conferences, seminars with universities abroad and hands-on workshops at the top end of each field. One seminar. Every campus. Live.
Amaravati Quantum Valley
Quantum is coming to Amaravati. So are we.

IBM Quantum System Two · 156 qubits · TCS · early 2027
Sources: McKinsey Quantum Technology Monitor 2025 · DST / PIB · IBM, YourStory 2026
And the future is arriving right here. Andhra Pradesh is building the Amaravati Quantum Valley, where IBM and TCS are installing a 156-qubit IBM Quantum System Two, India's largest quantum computer, with operations now targeted for early 2027. Why does it matter? Quantum computers can simulate molecules and materials that ordinary computers cannot, which means faster drug discovery and better batteries. They can search through millions of routes and schedules at once, which means optimised logistics. And they will change how networks are secured. McKinsey estimates quantum technology could be worth up to 97 billion dollars a year by 2035, and India has committed over six thousand crore rupees to its National Quantum Mission. The countries that use this technology first will grow fastest, and we intend to be among them. The question is whether our students will be spectators or builders. We will make sure they are ready to use it, build on it and lead with it. Quantum is coming to Amaravati. So are we.

Now the question every principal asks: who pays? Here is our answer. Everything you have seen today, Microsoft 365, the professional tools, training, the analytics and the 24-by-7 support, is one annual subscription per student. Lokha Institution Council will bear seventy to seventy-five percent of it, across every JNTU campus. The remaining twenty-five to thirty percent is the student's share, a fraction of what it would cost anyone to do this alone. We carry the bulk of the cost because we want every JNTU student to work with the same calibre of technology as a student at Oxford or Cambridge, and because we believe the return is enormous: for your students, for your placements, and for your institution's name. You focus on teaching. We carry the cost.
